stories.headline: After RMG, could the economy send more Bangladeshis back to the streets?
stories.summary: Garment workers blocked roads across Gazipur, Savar, Ashulia and Narayanganj for several days in early November, factories were vandalised, vehicles torched and the Border Guard Bangladesh deployed, with production suspended at 529 factories affecting nearly 987,000 workers. Point-to-point inflation stood at 8.34% in September, up from 8.26% in August, and the World Bank projects growth of only 3.4% in both FY2025-26 and FY2026-27.
stories.why_it_matters: The 529 factories, the 987,000 affected workers, the 8.34% inflation rate and the World Bank's 3.4% growth projection are the live numbers for any BCS/Bank answer on the garment unrest and the cost-of-living crisis — and the piece connects the unrest to the July Uprising's unresolved economic roots.
stories.exam_facts: Inflation has remained above 8% for years while wage growth has repeatedly failed to keep pace; the analysis says Bangladesh emerged from the July Uprising with a changed political order, but the two successive administrations inherited a broken economy left by the previous Awami regime, with the banking crisis unresolved, investment weak, energy shortages constraining production and the formal job market unable to absorb young people; the World Bank cites weaker investment, slowing exports and energy constraints behind its 3.4% projection; the piece warns the risk now looms over other sectors as the cost of living keeps rising.
stories.exam_relevance: Garment unrest, inflation, wage growth, World Bank growth projections, July Uprising economy — core BCS/Bank economy topics.

stories.headline: India declines comment on Hasina's possible return 'by military aircraft'
stories.summary: India has declined to comment on former prime minister Sheikh Hasina's possible return to Bangladesh through military arrangements. At a media briefing in New Delhi on 13 November, foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said his repeated references to the matter as a legal issue concern only the extradition process, adding: 'To the other part of your question, I have no comment to offer.'
stories.why_it_matters: Delhi's refusal to discuss the military-aircraft reports, while calling the matter a legal one only on extradition, is the latest hard fact for BCS/Bank questions on the Hasina extradition row and India-Bangladesh relations — and the two reported conditions frame the next round of the dispute.
stories.exam_facts: BBC Bangla reported on Thursday that India wanted Bangladesh's military to take responsibility for bringing Hasina back, preferably aboard a Bangladeshi military aircraft, and wanted assurances she could appeal against her death sentence and face a fresh trial over killings during the July 2024 uprising; the report, citing Indian government and military officials, said New Delhi set two conditions because Hasina's continued presence in India had become increasingly uncomfortable amid diplomatic and international pressure, while not wanting to appear to interfere in Bangladesh's independent judiciary; the foreign ministry said the next Dhaka-Delhi consular dialogue will be held on a mutually convenient date and will cover revised travel arrangements.
stories.exam_relevance: Extradition, India-Bangladesh relations, consular dialogue, judicial process — core BCS/Bank foreign-policy topics.

stories.headline: UK, Norway and Canada launch $10 billion climate finance initiative at COP31
stories.summary: Development finance institutions from Britain, Norway and Canada launched a joint initiative at COP31 in Antalya on 13 November to channel $10 billion into climate projects in emerging markets by 2030. Under a memorandum of understanding, British International Investment, Norway's Norfund and FinDev Canada will share investment pipelines, coordinate due diligence and cooperate on climate reporting.
stories.why_it_matters: A $10 billion joint facility from three state-backed lenders, with a 2030 deadline and named institutions, is the kind of concrete COP31 outcome BCS/Bank questions on climate finance ask for — and it shows how developing countries' calls for support are being answered.
stories.exam_facts: The $10 billion target includes private capital the partners expect to attract; funding will support renewable energy, electricity transmission and distribution grids, energy storage, sustainable fuels and industrial decarbonisation; UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham addressed the COP31 conference in Antalya on 12 November; the initiative comes as developing countries most exposed to climate disasters press for support while Western governments face competing priorities including national security and rising living costs.
stories.exam_relevance: Climate finance, COP31, development finance institutions, renewable energy investment — core BCS/Bank environment and international topics.

stories.headline: Fire at NCP MP Nusrat Tabassum's Kushtia home: petrol-bomb claim, parliament row, probe under way
stories.summary: A fire broke out at the ancestral home of NCP leader and reserved-seat MP Nusrat Tabassum in Bagoan village, Daulatpur, Kushtia, in the small hours of 12 November. NCP leaders say videos purporting to be CCTV footage are consistent with a petrol bomb attack, while Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed told parliament he believed no petrol bomb was used and a short circuit from old wiring was highly likely.
stories.why_it_matters: A fire at an MP's home, a petrol-bomb allegation against banned Awami League affiliates, a minister contradicting it in parliament and a rural electricity official ruling out a short circuit are the live facts for BCS/Bank questions on law and order, political violence and the July uprising's aftermath.
stories.exam_facts: Opposition Chief Whip Nahid Islam told parliament four petrol bombs had been thrown at the house and warned that if NCP families were attacked, BNP families would be next; a Kushtia rural electricity official, Tozammel Haque, inspected the meter, wiring and main switch and said the cut-out was intact, the transformer fuse had not blown and the main switch was undamaged, so there was no possibility of a short circuit; a four-member probe committee formed by the Ministry of Home Affairs visited the house at around 10:30 am on 13 November and questioned residents; Nusrat filed a case at Daulatpur police station alleging attempted murder through arson and an explosion, naming leaders of the banned Bangladesh Chhatra League, Jubo League and Swechchhasebak League; NCP leaders inspected the house on 13 November, found the meter and wiring apparently intact, and said they would publish a report; the home minister said a joint investigation by the Border Guard Bangladesh, fire service, administration and police was under way and action would follow if sabotage was established.
stories.exam_relevance: Political violence, law and order, parliamentary debate, investigation process — core BCS/Bank politics and governance topics.

stories.headline: DU, JU and BUET shut doors on HSC supplementary candidates; most other universities adjust schedules
stories.summary: The University of Dhaka and Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology are not allowing students who pass the HSC supplementary examinations to sit for undergraduate admission tests, sticking to previously announced schedules, while most other universities are revising theirs. Of the 1,240,798 candidates who sat the HSC under 11 boards, 646,685 passed — a 52.12% pass rate — and 40,084 secured GPA-5.
stories.why_it_matters: A 52.12% pass rate, nearly half the candidates failing, supplementary exams for up to two subjects, and DU and BUET refusing supplementary passers while Chittagong and Rajshahi adjust are the live education facts for candidates and for BCS/Bank questions on admissions and education policy.
stories.exam_facts: The HSC and equivalent results were published on 31 October; supplementary examinations for students who failed in up to two subjects run from 1 December to 15 December, with results expected by late December; a University Grants Commission meeting on Monday decided public universities will begin accepting first-year applications from January, with admission tests from February; the University of Chittagong will accept online applications from 10 December to 10 January, with tests from 29 January to 8 February, and supplementary passers may register on the portal before their results; the University of Rajshahi will hold tests from 12 February, with applications from 15 November to 30 November, and supplementary passers get seven days to apply after their results; education stakeholders have urged universities that already announced test dates to reconsider.
stories.exam_relevance: HSC examinations, supplementary examinations, university admissions, UGC coordination — core BCS/Bank education topics.

stories.headline: From Kalabogi to COP31: columnist argues developed nations must take responsibility for the climate crisis
stories.summary: Columnist Naim-Ul-Karim Sanchaya writes from Kalabogi, a 'hanging' village on the Shibsa River in Dacope, Khulna, where homes on thatched and bamboo structures must be relocated several times a year as river erosion takes the land. He argues the central question at COP31 is who bears responsibility, and the answer is unambiguous: developed nations, whose historical emissions created the crisis, must take primary responsibility — 'not as charity, but as justice'.
stories.why_it_matters: The Kalabogi case — a village that moves several times a year — gives BCS/Bank candidates the human anchor for climate-justice answers, and the column's numbers (over 170 million people, under 0.5% of emissions, $300 billion promised by 2035) are the quotable core of Bangladesh's COP31 position.
stories.exam_facts: The columnist writes that Bangladesh, with over 170 million people, contributes less than 0.5% of global emissions yet sits on the frontlines of sea-level rise, salinity intrusion and increasingly violent cyclones; he argues the United States, which has again declined to attend the negotiations, cannot ignore its role as the world's largest historical emitter, while China and other emerging economies have responsibilities that differ in scale and timing; he writes that developed countries promised to mobilise $300 billion a year by 2035 to help vulnerable nations adapt, but that promises made at climate summits have a way of evaporating when the cameras leave; he says Bangladesh's environment minister has made clear poorer countries are paying the heaviest price for emissions largely generated by rich nations.
stories.exam_relevance: Climate justice, COP31, historical emissions, loss and damage, LDC climate diplomacy — core BCS/Bank environment topics.

stories.headline: Bangladesh presses for affordable climate finance at COP31 as Climate Investment Funds pledges $30m
stories.summary: Bangladesh's delegation at COP31, led by Environment Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo, told a press briefing on 13 November that low-carbon development and the energy transition depend on predictable and affordable international finance. Under its NDC 3.0, Bangladesh targets a 6.39% emissions cut below business-as-usual by 2035 from domestic resources, plus a further 13.92% conditional on international support — and the Climate Investment Funds has selected Bangladesh for up to $30 million for coastal protection and mangrove restoration.
stories.why_it_matters: The NDC 3.0 numbers (6.39% unconditional, 13.92% conditional), the $120 billion-a-year LDC adaptation demand and the $30 million CIF pledge are the exact figures for BCS/Bank questions on Bangladesh's climate negotiating position at COP31.
stories.exam_facts: The first four days of formal negotiations had concluded with several key agenda items still unresolved and no final outcomes reached; Bangladesh is working with the Least Developed Countries Group, the G77 and China for a balanced and ambitious outcome; the delegation called for the LDC Group's demand of $120 billion a year in adaptation funding before 2035, a clear pathway for pledged finance, and funding that reaches local communities; Bangladesh is pursuing rooftop solar, tree planting and canal restoration; the delegation raised concerns about the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism and urged faster implementation of National Adaptation Plans and more resources for the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage; the $30 million CIF funding was announced on Thursday at the Bangladesh Pavilion, where Bangladesh is among the first five countries to receive it, and the government is advancing preparations for international carbon credit trading; the World Meteorological Organization's 2026 update put the global average temperature for January to September at about 1.47°C above pre-industrial levels.
stories.exam_relevance: COP31 negotiations, NDC 3.0, climate finance, adaptation funding, carbon markets — core BCS/Bank environment and foreign-policy topics.
stories.key_people: Abdul Awal Mintoo, Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister; Dr Md Saimum Parvez, Prime Minister's Special Assistant on Environment; Shama Obaid Islam, State Minister for Foreign Affairs; Sheikh Faridul Islam, State Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change

stories.headline: Healthcare decentralisation can work if staff and funds follow the equipment, columnist argues
stories.summary: Columnist Dr Syed Abdul Hamid writes that the Upazila Governance and Development Project, which ran from FY2015-16 to 31 December 2025, delivered more than 47,000 medical works, items and supplies across 408 upazilas, and an assessment of 158 upazilas found 91.88% of the 29,257 items distributed there operational. But he argues the same assessment exposed 'structural friction': 8.11% of the equipment — 2,375 units — was non-functional or underutilised, largely because specialists and funds did not follow the hardware.
stories.why_it_matters: The UGDP numbers (47,000 items, 408 upazilas, 91.88% operational, 8.11% idle) and the 'No Staff, No Stuff' prescription are the hard facts for BCS/Bank answers on rural healthcare, decentralisation and public-sector project design.
stories.exam_facts: The columnist writes that high-performing upazilas received typically Tk50 lakh a year on top of their Annual Development Programme block allocation, and upazilas invested over Tk113 crore in diagnostic tools and facility upgrades through decentralised procurement; he writes that anaesthesia machines sit idle without sanctioned junior anaesthesia consultants, X-ray and ultrasound units gather dust without radiologists, and ambulances arrive without trained drivers or fuel budgets, while repairs costing under Tk20,000 can sideline a machine for months; he argues over half of physician posts at many upazila health complexes are vacant in some divisions and Bangladesh's health workforce density remains below World Health Organization recommendations; his prescriptions include a 'No Staff, No Stuff' mandate, a Joint Human Resource Mapping Protocol between the health and local government ministries, rural retention incentives, ring-fencing diagnostic income for repairs, bundling a year's consumables and long-term warranties into procurement, and a second phase of the project pledged during the prime minister's visit to Japan.
stories.exam_relevance: Rural healthcare, decentralisation, upazila governance, health workforce, public procurement — core BCS/Bank health and governance topics.
stories.key_people: Dr Syed Abdul Hamid, professor, Institute of Health Economics, University of Dhaka

stories.headline: Energy crisis hits home in the kitchen as gas rationing and LPG prices bite, columnist writes
stories.summary: Columnist Nahian Rahman writes that Bangladesh's gas supply generally hovers around 2.6 billion cubic feet per day, forcing Petrobangla to ration gas across power plants, industries and households. The two floating LNG terminals at Moheshkhali were repeatedly disrupted — Excelerate's terminal was knocked offline by a fire in July and suffered another fault in August — and a 12 kg LPG cylinder that cost Tk1,837 in October was raised by Tk223 to Tk2,060 on 2 November, while buyers report paying Tk2,200 or more.
stories.why_it_matters: The 2.6 billion cubic feet of gas a day, the Tk2,060 official LPG price against Tk2,200 paid on the street, and the Tk41,000 crore power subsidy are the live numbers for BCS/Bank answers on the energy crisis — and the column shows how it reaches the kitchen, not just the factory.
stories.exam_facts: The columnist writes that Summit's terminal suspended regasification for maintenance from 4 to 7 November, temporarily reducing supplies to the national grid; he writes that induction cookers use roughly 30% less power than conventional electric heating, while infrared units can cost nearly double to run; under the June residential tariff schedule, units between 301 and 400 cost Tk9.62 and units between 401 and 600 cost Tk15.01, and the June 3 order raised the weighted average retail tariff from Tk9.11 to Tk10.63 per unit — a 16.68% rise — before the lowest tiers were restored, bringing the average to Tk10.40; the regulator's chairman acknowledged no assessment had been conducted of the increase's impact on inflation or household expenditure; the government is still expected to provide around Tk41,000 crore in annual subsidy to the Bangladesh Power Development Board in FY2026-27; Excelerate Energy declared force majeure in March amid the Middle East conflict, suspending contracted LNG deliveries, and was expected to deliver one cargo in October after a seven-month interruption.
stories.exam_relevance: Energy crisis, LNG terminals, gas rationing, LPG pricing, electricity tariffs, subsidies — core BCS/Bank economy topics.
stories.key_people: Nahian Rahman, research associate, Bangladesh Institute of Governance and Management (BIGM)

stories.headline: Seven in 10 people with diabetes in Bangladesh unaware of the condition
stories.summary: Around 70% of people with diabetes in Bangladesh are unaware they have the disease, according to the Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey 2022: 67% of women and 72% of men with diabetes did not know they had high blood glucose, up from 59% and 61% in 2017-18. The International Diabetes Federation's Diabetes Atlas-2025 puts the number of adults aged 20-79 living with diabetes in Bangladesh at around 1.39 crore in 2024.
stories.why_it_matters: The 70% unaware, the 1.39 crore adults with diabetes and the 127% rise in registered patients are the headline health numbers for World Diabetes Day — and the urban-rural and wealth gaps are exactly the inequality facts BCS/Bank health questions use.
stories.exam_facts: The BDHS 2022, covering 30,018 households, found 17% of women and 15% of men aged 18 and above had diabetes, up from 10% and 11% in 2017-18; the Diabetic Association of Bangladesh registered 30.61 lakh patients in 2014-15 and 69.37 lakh in 2024-25, a rise of 127%, with 3.83 lakh new patients in 2024-25; prevalence was 24% among urban women against 14% among rural women, and 26% among women in the highest wealth quintile against 11% in the lowest; only 6% of female patients and 5% of male patients were aware of their condition, taking medication and with blood glucose under control, while 9% of both had elevated blood glucose but took no medication; doctors say sedentary lifestyles, unhealthy diets, urbanisation and genetic predisposition drive the rise, and lifestyle changes alone can prevent around 58-60% of diabetes cases among people at risk; the country is observing World Diabetes Day on 14 November with the theme 'Early action on diabetes'.
stories.exam_relevance: Public health, diabetes, health surveys, urban-rural inequality, non-communicable diseases — core BCS/Bank health topics.
stories.key_people: Prof Sharmin Jahan, chairman, Endocrinology and Metabolism, Bangladesh Medical University; Prof Prabath Chandra Biswas, Director General, Directorate General of Health Services; Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain, Health Minister

stories.headline: Jail terms, fines proposed for creating content by harassing animals
stories.summary: Draft amendments to the Animal Welfare Act, 2019 propose up to six months in prison or a fine of Tk50,000, or both, for creating and publishing content by harassing animals — and for assisting in such production. The offence would be cognisable. The move follows viral videos, including a Facebook page's drone footage of a frightened fox that was viewed 781,000 times and a video of a sleeping dog harassed with balloons that drew nearly 500,000 views.
stories.why_it_matters: A six-month jail term and Tk50,000 fine for animal-harassment content, a new cognisable offence, and the viral-video trigger are the testable facts of a new law — and the case shows how social-media content creation is entering Bangladesh's statute book.
stories.exam_facts: The Animal Welfare Act, 2019 had 14 sub-sections under Section 6; the proposed amendment adds sub-section (ণ), covering content made by harassing animals, frightening them with reflections or by attaching objects to their bodies; more than 100 Facebook pages and profiles carry such videos, and the 'Banglar Drone' page alone has over 100 videos made by harassing foxes and their families; seven types of offences are proposed to become cognisable and non-bailable; the Department of Livestock Services has sent the draft amendments to the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock, which has published them on its website for stakeholder opinions before sending the draft to the Ministry of Law for vetting.
stories.exam_relevance: Animal welfare law, social media regulation, draft legislation, cognisable offences — BCS/Bank law and governance topics.
stories.key_people: Md Shahzaman Khan, Acting Director General, Department of Livestock Services
stories.figures: Up to 6 months in prison or Tk50,000 fine; fox video 781,000 views; dog video nearly 500,000 views; over 100 pages and profiles; over 100 videos on one page; Section 6, 14 sub-sections.

stories.headline: Tourists flock to Cheradia despite restrictions, raising biodiversity concerns
stories.summary: Tourists are visiting Cheradia, at the southern tip of Saint Martin's Island, every day despite a ban, walking or riding easy-bikes, motorcycles and bicycles from Madhyardia, and crushing red crabs, snails and clams underfoot while damaging coral and algae. Department of Environment volunteers are too few to enforce the rules, although the island is an ecologically critical area with a 1,743 sq km marine protected area and a cap of 3,500 overnight tourists a day.
stories.why_it_matters: Saint Martin's is Bangladesh's only coral island, an ecologically critical area since 1999 with a 1,743 sq km marine protected area — and the gap between the 3,500-a-day cap and the enforcement on the ground is the live fact for BCS/Bank questions on conservation versus tourism.
stories.exam_facts: Saint Martin's Island covers about eight square kilometres in the Bay of Bengal; the government declared the whole island an Ecologically Critical Area in 1999 and a 1,743-square-kilometre area of the Bay of Bengal around it a Marine Protected Area in January 2023; collecting coral and stones, destroying keya forests, cutting trees, plucking fruits and dumping waste are prohibited, with violations carrying up to 10 years' imprisonment or a fine of up to Tk1 million; the government has kept the island open to tourists from 1 November to 15 March, with a maximum of 3,500 tourists a day staying overnight, and vessels began operating on 5 November, carrying an average of 2,000 tourists a day on three vessels after a 120-kilometre sea journey from Cox's Bazar; a 12-point guideline bans loud noise on the beach, littering with plastic, late-night gatherings that disturb nesting sea turtles, entering keya forests and driving easy-bikes onto the sand.
stories.exam_relevance: Conservation, ecologically critical areas, marine protected areas, tourism management — core BCS/Bank environment and geography topics.
stories.figures: Island about 8 sq km; ECA declared 1999; 1,743 sq km Marine Protected Area (January 2023); penalty up to 10 years or Tk1 million; season 1 November-15 March; cap 3,500 tourists a day; about 2,000 a day on 3 vessels; 120 km by sea from Cox's Bazar.
